name: Single jersey
summary: Single jersey is a plain knit with visibly different front and back surfaces.
construction: One set of needles forms connected loops. The face shows the legs of the stitches; the reverse shows their rounded crowns.
recognize: Look for small V shapes in vertical columns on the face and a more bumpy reverse.
distinguish: Jersey names a construction, not a fiber. Interlock has a different double-knit structure and more similar surfaces.

references.title: Craft Yarn Council: How to Read a Knitting Pattern

name: Rib knit
summary: Rib knit alternates face and reverse stitch columns to form expandable lengthwise ribs.
construction: In 1 × 1 rib, a face column alternates with a reverse column. Other arrangements, such as 2 × 2, group the columns into wider ribs.
recognize: Gently stretch across the ribs to reveal the recessed columns between them.
distinguish: A woven rib is an interlacing effect; rib knitting is built from loops.

references.title: Craft Yarn Council: Certified Knitting Instructors Program

name: Interlock
summary: Interlock is a double knit with a smooth, similar appearance on both sides.
construction: Opposing needle sets work in alternating selections. Two yarn feeds complete one course of this interlocking structure.
recognize: Both surfaces show fine knit columns rather than the contrasting face and back of single jersey.
distinguish: Interlock is one specific double-knit construction; double knit does not always mean interlock.

name: Ponte di Roma
summary: Ponte is a firm double knit with a subtle horizontal rib.
construction: Its repeat combines interlock knitting with courses worked on each needle set separately. This produces a compact fabric with similar faces.
recognize: Look for fine crosswise lines on a smooth, substantial knit.
distinguish: Ponte is a knit, even when tailored like woven cloth.

name: Piqué knit
summary: Piqué knit combines knit and tuck stitches to produce a small cellular surface.
construction: Some needles hold loops while others knit, creating the texture. Single, double and six-feed piqués use different repeats, so their faces and thicknesses vary.
recognize: Look for a fine dimpled or honeycomb-like texture, familiar from polo shirts.
distinguish: Knitted piqué and woven piqué share a name but use different construction methods.

name: French terry
summary: French terry pairs a jersey face with an unbrushed looped back.
construction: A backing yarn forms floats behind the face. These remain unnapped, preserving the looped surface.
recognize: Turn it over to see distinct loops rather than a fuzzy nap.
distinguish: Woven toweling terry uses a different loop-forming construction.

name: Sweatshirt fleece
summary: Sweatshirt fleece has a smooth knit face and a raised, fuzzy backing.
construction: Backing yarns are knitted into the cloth. Napping raises their fibers to form the soft interior.
recognize: The reverse looks brushed rather than distinctly looped.
distinguish: This entry describes sweatshirt construction; fleece also names other pile fabrics and raw sheep wool.

name: Jacquard knit
summary: Jacquard knitting uses selected stitches and yarns to build pattern into a knit.
construction: Machine needle selection controls where colors or textures appear. Single-knit and double-knit versions manage the unused yarns differently.
recognize: Inspect the reverse as well as the face: the design is made in the stitches, not simply printed over them.
distinguish: Jacquard is a patterning method, not one motif or fiber; knitted and woven jacquards are structurally different.

name: Tricot
summary: Tricot is a warp-knit family often made as fine, relatively flat fabric.
construction: Many lengthwise yarns are guided into interconnected loops. Tricot machines commonly produce fine structures with relatively simple patterning.
recognize: Look for fine loop columns and a different reverse texture; a close inspection is more useful than stretch alone.
distinguish: Warp knitting uses many lengthwise yarns; weft knitting builds courses from yarn fed across the fabric.

name: Raschel
summary: Raschel is a versatile warp-knitting family used for meshes, lace and other textured fabrics.
construction: Guide bars position lengthwise yarns around needles to make interlinked loops. Machine configuration and yarn selection allow both open and denser designs.
recognize: An open net or lace-like surface may be raschel, but appearance alone cannot confirm the machine type.
distinguish: Raschel names a knitting family, not a single mesh pattern or all lace.

name: Garter stitch
summary: Garter stitch makes a reversible knit with pronounced horizontal ridges.
construction: When working flat, knitting every row forms garter stitch. The fabric alternates how the rows face the viewer, rather than presenting only knit faces on one side.
recognize: Look for stacked horizontal ridges with a similar appearance on both surfaces.
distinguish: Knitting every round in circular work produces stockinette, so flat-row instructions cannot be transferred unchanged.

references.title: Craft Yarn Council: How to Read a Knitting Pattern
Craft Yarn Council: Learn Knit Stitch

name: Seed stitch
summary: Seed stitch alternates knit and purl stitches into a small, pebbled texture.
construction: Knit and purl stitches alternate across a row. On subsequent rows, their placement reverses rather than stacking into rib columns.
recognize: Small raised bumps are distributed across both sides without long vertical ribs.
distinguish: Moss stitch terminology varies by region; inspect the written repeat rather than assuming every moss pattern equals seed stitch.

references.title: Craft Yarn Council: Certified Knitting Instructors Program
Yarnspirations: How to Seed Stitch Knitting

name: Cable knit
summary: Cable knitting crosses groups of stitches to make raised ropes, braids or traveling lines.
construction: Some stitches are held in front or behind while neighboring stitches are worked. Working the held stitches afterward changes their order and creates a crossing.
recognize: Follow the raised stitch columns through their repeated crossings.
distinguish: An Aran-style sweater may combine cables with several other textures; cable knit does not describe the whole tradition.

references.title: Craft Yarn Council: Cable Knit Turtleneck
V&A: Knitting Traditions of the British Isles and Ireland

name: Intarsia knitting
summary: Intarsia forms separate color areas without carrying each unused yarn across the whole reverse.
construction: Each color area has its own yarn supply. Neighboring areas connect where the yarns change, forming the image within the knitted fabric.
recognize: Large color blocks have local joins at their boundaries rather than long backing floats.
distinguish: Stranded colorwork carries unused colors behind the active stitches; intarsia treats the color areas separately.

name: Fair Isle knitting
summary: Fair Isle is a Shetland colorwork tradition using stranded yarns and repeating knitted motifs.
construction: Typically two colors are worked within each row or round. The unused yarn travels behind the stitches as short floats, while colors can change between bands.
recognize: Look for repeating bands of small motifs and colored floats on the reverse.
distinguish: Not every stranded multicolor knit is Fair Isle; the name also carries a specific regional design tradition.

references.title: Shetland Museum: Beginners Fair Isle Knitting
Shetland Heritage Shop: Fair Isle Knitting

name: Pointelle
summary: Pointelle uses small deliberate openings to pattern a knitted surface.
construction: In machine pointelle, selected stitches move to neighboring needles. Knitting resumes at the emptied positions, leaving patterned holes.
recognize: Repeated eyelets interrupt the knit, often arranged into lines or small geometric figures.
distinguish: These openings are created during knitting; embroidered eyelet and cutwork use a different process on a ground fabric.

references.title: STOLL: Training of Manual Flat Knitting Machine, Pointelle

name: Bouclé texture
summary: Bouclé texture comes from a fancy yarn with loops or curls along its length.
construction: An effect yarn is fed differently from the supporting yarns during twisting. Its extra length produces the irregular looped texture before the yarn becomes cloth.
recognize: Look for curled yarn projections rather than a uniform cut pile.
distinguish: Bouclé is a yarn effect used in both woven and knitted fabrics, not one weave or finishing operation.

name: Slub texture
summary: Slub texture uses thicker sections along a yarn to create an uneven surface.
construction: A decorative slub yarn deliberately includes localized thick places. Their spacing and size influence the texture of the finished woven or knitted cloth.
recognize: Look for short thick streaks that follow individual yarns.
distinguish: An uneven appearance alone cannot establish fiber content or whether the variation was intentional.

name: Brushed surface
summary: Brushing raises surface fibers to change a fabric's appearance and feel.
construction: A formed fabric undergoes mechanical surface treatment. The raised fibers can soften the outline of the original weave or knit.
recognize: Look for a light fibrous halo above the underlying structure.
distinguish: Brushing does not specify a fiber or weave. Technical finishing terminology distinguishes brushing from napping and abrasive sueding.

name: Sueded finish
summary: Sueding gives fabric a fine, suede-like surface through controlled abrasion.
construction: Fabric passes against abrasive rollers, commonly covered with a sandpaper-like surface. This modifies the exposed fibers rather than making a new woven or knitted structure.
recognize: Look for a short, fine surface fuzz and muted luster.
distinguish: Suede-like textile finishing does not make fabric into leather; commercial peach and suede finishes vary in intensity.

name: Embossed texture
summary: Embossing presses a relief pattern into an existing fabric surface.
construction: Engraved rollers apply pressure and sometimes heat. How well the effect lasts depends on the fibers and the setting or finishing treatment.
recognize: Raised and recessed areas repeat across an otherwise continuous base fabric.
distinguish: An embossed texture can imitate a woven effect without using that weave; inspect the underlying yarn arrangement.

name: Moiré finish
summary: Moiré describes a rippling, watered appearance on a fabric surface.
construction: A traditional route uses pressure during calendering to alter how parts of the fabric reflect light. The finished effect lies over the underlying fabric structure.
recognize: Look for irregular flowing bands of light and dark, like watermarks.
distinguish: Moiré is not necessarily silk, and a printed imitation or camera interference pattern does not establish a moiré finish.

name: Burnout / devoré
summary: Burnout creates sheer patterns by selectively removing one fiber component from a fabric.
construction: A chemical print acts on a susceptible component in a blend. The remaining component supports the more open areas of the design.
recognize: Opaque and translucent areas form a deliberate pattern within the same cloth.
distinguish: Devoré is a subtractive treatment, not a fiber, weave or ordinary color print.

name: Flocked surface
summary: Flocking attaches short fibers to a surface to create a soft, raised design.
construction: Adhesive is applied in the desired pattern. Short cut fibers are deposited into it, then the adhesive is fixed to hold them in place.
recognize: A pile-like motif sits on top of a distinct base fabric.
distinguish: Flock is added to a substrate; woven or knitted pile is incorporated while the fabric is formed.

references.title: Cotton Incorporated: Printing Booklet, Flock Printing

name: Bobbin lace
summary: Bobbin lace creates openwork by crossing and twisting multiple threads.
construction: Threads wound on bobbins are worked around a pattern. Pins on a supporting pillow hold the developing network in place.
recognize: Close inspection reveals interlaced thread paths forming the solid and open areas.
distinguish: Needle lace builds its structure with a needle and thread; many machine laces imitate either appearance.

references.title: The Lace Guild: Origins and History
The Met: Textile Production in Europe, Lace

name: Needle lace
summary: Needle lace builds an openwork fabric using a needle and thread.
construction: Stitches connect to one another and to supporting outline threads. The resulting network forms lace rather than merely decorating an intact ground cloth.
recognize: Look for fine stitched mesh and denser stitched areas joined into a self-supporting design.
distinguish: Needle lace, bobbin lace and knitted lace can look related while their thread structures differ.

references.title: The Lace Guild: Origins and History
The Met: Gems of European Lace

name: Crochet
summary: Crochet forms fabric by drawing yarn through loops with a hook.
construction: Chains establish a starting structure and stitches build into earlier stitches or spaces. Different stitch heights and placements create dense cloth or open motifs.
recognize: Trace the chains and stitch posts; crochet may be worked in rows, rounds or joined motifs.
distinguish: Hand crochet differs from knitting; industrial machinery also uses the term crochet for some warp-knitted structures.

name: Macramé
summary: Macramé builds decorative textiles through arrangements of knots.
construction: Lengths of cord or thread are knotted together. Repeated knots and deliberately open spaces form the design without a woven warp-and-weft grid.
recognize: Visible knots anchor the cord network, often with loose lengths continuing as fringe.
distinguish: A knotted textile can resemble open weaving or crochet, but its connections are tied knots.

references.title: Cooper Hewitt: Sample Card of Macramé

name: Embroidery
summary: Embroidery creates decoration through stitches worked on or through a supporting material.
construction: Threads may follow counted positions in the ground or move freely over a drawn design. Additional techniques attach laid threads or build raised details.
recognize: Look for decorative stitches that can be distinguished from the ground fabric's own yarn structure.
distinguish: This is a broad family of techniques; similar motifs can also be printed or woven.

references.title: V&A: Embroidery Styles, an Illustrated Guide

name: Quilting
summary: Quilting joins fabric layers with lines of stitching that can also form a surface design.
construction: Stitches pass through the layers, often including padding between a face and backing. Their layout controls how the layers are held and where raised areas remain.
recognize: Follow the stitched channels separating the fuller areas between them.
distinguish: Patchwork joins pieces into a surface; quilting joins layers, and a quilt need not contain patchwork.

references.title: V&A: An Introduction to Quilting and Patchwork

name: Smocking
summary: Smocking gathers cloth into small folds held and decorated by stitches.
construction: A wide area of fabric is gathered into regular pleats. Stitches connect selected folds to control fullness and make a textured pattern.
recognize: Look for stitch-linked pleats forming compact geometric areas beside looser cloth.
distinguish: Honeycomb smocking describes one arrangement; a woven honeycomb texture does not use this gathering technique.

name: Pleated texture
summary: Pleating folds an existing fabric into a repeated three-dimensional shape.
construction: Folds may be formed in fabric before cutting or in an already sewn garment. Industrial methods can use heat to set suitable fibers into the desired shape.
recognize: Look for repeated folds that change depth or open as the cloth moves.
distinguish: Pleats describe fabric shaping, not a weave; their permanence and care requirements depend on the specific product.

references.title: ISSEY MIYAKE: Pleated Product Care and Construction
National Art Center, Tokyo: Miyake Issey Exhibition
